opus-5.5.text:
I think the cleanest way to see it is to start from the data, because the architecture follows from the data.

Nemotron lives in the digital world. Its native input and output is language: tokens that humans already compressed into symbols. Text is extremely information-dense, it's discrete, and the internet has given us an enormous amount of it. So the architectural question there is mostly about scaling reasoning: how do you make a transformer think longer and more efficiently, use tools, follow instructions, and be cheap enough to deploy? That's why you see work on hybrid architectures, mixing attention with state-space layers, mixture-of-experts, and long-context efficiency. The world it reasons about is already described in words.

Physical AI starts from a very different place. Our input is photons, and eventually our output is torque, motor commands. Video is high-dimensional, continuous, and highly redundant. One second of video has a huge number of pixels but relatively little new information. So the first architectural problem is not reasoning, it's representation. You need a very good tokenizer, continuous or discrete, that compresses space and time without throwing away the physics. If your tokenizer loses the fact that a cup's handle is rigid, no amount of model scale downstream will recover it.

The second difference is what the model is predicting. A language model predicts the next token, and that has worked remarkably well. A world model has to predict how the world evolves, often conditioned on an action: if the robot pushes here, what happens next? That's why in our Cosmos work we've explored both diffusion-based and autoregressive world models. Diffusion is very good at producing high-fidelity, physically coherent video. Autoregressive models fit naturally with the LLM stack and with interaction. I don't think the field has settled on one answer, and I suspect the answer will be a combination.

Third, in the physical world you can't fix mistakes by simply regenerating. Physics doesn't give you an undo button. So we care a lot about things like 3D consistency, object permanence, and causality, properties that are almost free in text because language already abstracts them away, but that a video model has to actually learn.

That said, I don't see these as two separate worlds that stay apart. They're converging. A physical AI system needs language and reasoning. When you tell a robot "clean up the kitchen," something has to understand that, plan, and reason about common sense, and that's where a reasoning model like the Nemotron family, or a vision-language reasoning model like Cosmos Reason, comes in. And going the other way, digital agents increasingly benefit from grounding in the physical world. So in the long run I think of it as a stack: a reasoning brain that's very good at symbols, a world model that understands how the physical world evolves, and a policy that acts. Today they look architecturally different because their data is different. Over time, I expect the boundary to get blurrier, and the interesting research is exactly at that boundary.

Physical AI is described in terms of video, world models, and action-conditioned prediction.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and I think the easiest way to understand it is to start from what each model is actually trying to predict.

Nemotron, like most of the language-model family, lives in a digital world. Its training data is text, code, and increasingly images and documents that humans created. The thing it's modeling is essentially human knowledge and human intent as expressed through symbols. It can be extremely smart about reasoning, about following instructions, about writing a program. But the world it's in is a world that humans already abstracted. Someone turned reality into words before the model ever saw it.

What my team works on, with Cosmos, is different. We're trying to model the physical world itself, before anyone has abstracted it. The input is sensor data: video, depth, sometimes multiple cameras from a robot or a car, plus the actions the agent took. And the question the model has to answer isn't "what word comes next," it's "what will the world look like in the next fraction of a second if I move my arm this way, or if this pedestrian keeps walking." So the fundamental object you're predicting is a future state of the environment, not a token of language.

That difference pushes the architectures in different directions. A few things stand out to me.

First, the tokenizer. In language, tokenization is almost a solved problem. For video, it's one of the hardest parts. You have to compress pixels across space and time into something a transformer can work with, without losing the physics. If your tokenizer blurs away the small motion that tells you an object is about to slide off a table, the model can't learn that physics no matter how big it is. So we spend a lot of effort on the tokenizer, both discrete and continuous versions, and that just isn't a concern in the same way on the digital side.

Second, time and causality. Language models are autoregressive over a sequence, and that works. For the physical world, you need a notion of time that respects causality, where the future depends on the past and on actions, and you also often want to generate in a way that's consistent over long horizons. So we end up using a mixture of diffusion-style generation for visual fidelity and autoregressive structure for temporal causality. Nemotron is almost purely autoregressive, and that's the right choice for text.

Third, conditioning on actions. A language model is conditioned on a prompt. A world model has to be conditioned on controls: steering angle, joint torques, a trajectory. That's a different interface. The model is, in a sense, a simulator you can drive, not a conversation partner.

Fourth, the data regime is completely different. The internet gives you trillions of tokens of text. Physical interaction data is scarce and expensive. You can't scrape a million hours of a humanoid picking up cups. So a lot of our design is about data efficiency, about curating and filtering video at enormous scale, and about synthetic data generation, where the world model itself becomes a data factory for the policy models.

Having said all that, I actually don't see them as opposed. I see them converging in an interesting way. A physical AI system needs both. It needs the Nemotron-style brain for high-level reasoning: understanding what the task is, planning, talking to a person. And it needs the world model for low-level grounding: understanding what will happen physically, and verifying that the plan is feasible before acting. Our reasoning variants of Cosmos are explicitly trying to bring some of that language-model capability into the physical side, where the model can look at a video and reason about it in words, and then also predict what happens next.

So the way I'd put it is: Nemotron is a model of what humans have said about the world. Cosmos is a model of how the world actually behaves. The architecture differences follow directly from that. And the really exciting work right now is in the interface between the two, where the reasoning model can use the world model as its imagination.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame the difference around what the model needs to understand and what its outputs need to accomplish. A digital-world model operates primarily through language, code, and other digital representations. For Physical AI, the model also needs to understand space, motion, and how actions change the world over time.

That changes the architectural requirements. You need to connect perception with temporal reasoning and action, and you need some way to represent physical dynamics. A useful prediction is not simply what comes next in a sequence, but what might happen if an agent takes a particular action.

I wouldn’t draw a hard boundary between the two, though. They can share foundational components. The distinction is how those components are organized and trained: toward producing useful digital outputs, or toward understanding and interacting with a physical environment. Without getting into specific implementations, that’s the architectural shift I’d emphasize.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difference is what the model has to understand and what it has to produce. For a digital-world model like Nemotron, much of the interaction happens through language and other digital representations. With Physical AI, the model needs to connect perception to action: what is happening around me, how might it change, and what should I do next?

That pushes the architecture toward representations of space, time, motion, and actions. It also makes the feedback loop important. An action changes the environment, and the next observation tells you whether your prediction was right.

But I wouldn’t draw a hard boundary between the two. Reasoning and language can be useful in a physical system. The question is how you connect those capabilities to a model of the world and to actions that work under physical constraints.
